terms.gloss: and so forth, and the rest
terms.grammar: phrase: the neuter plural of cēterus; also cēteraque, or cētera alone
evidence: Cic. Att. 10.15.4: dum pānis et cētera in nāvem parantur
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: used when one refers to something well known in a few words, or names only a few of many things; Cicero also ends a quotation with it. A list may end with cētera and no “and” (fundum, aedēs, parietem, supellectilem, penus, cētera, Cic. Top. 27). Cēterī are the others (see the others).

evidence: Cic. Fam. 2.10.2: hīcine est ille, quī urbem? quem senātus? nōstī cētera.
terms.comment: Breaks off a well-known story or quotation, leaving the hearer to finish it.

terms.gloss: and so on (in order), one after another
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.160 (Lewis & Short): prīma diīs immortālibus, secunda patriae, tertia parentibus, deinceps gradātim reliqua reliquīs
terms.comment: After a series counted out, “and so on down the line”; its plain sense is “one after another, next in order” (Lewis & Short).
Perinde is “in the same manner, just as, equally” (Lewis & Short), mostly with ac, ut or quasi; it does not close a list. Traupman 271 gives et cētera beside it.

phrases.latin: ego, dum pānis et cētera in nāvem parantur, excurrō in Pompejānum.
phrases.english: While the bread and so on are being got on board, I’m running over to my house at Pompeii.

phrases.latin: hīcine est ille, quī urbem? quem senātus? nōstī cētera.
phrases.english: Is this the man who (saved) the city? Whom the senate (honoured)? You know the rest.

sources: Lewis & Short: ceterus · Lewis & Short: deinceps
Cic. Att. 10.15.4, Fam. 2.10.2 and 7.28.2 checked against the Perseus Latin texts (11 November 2026).
